questions.q: What does an anthropologist study? Give one example of something an anthropologist could study.
questions.a: An anthropologist studies human societies and cultures, from the oldest times to the present. Example: the customs and festivals of a tribal community living today (or the way of life of a community long ago).
s: States that an anthropologist studies human societies and cultures from the oldest times to the present
Gives one fitting example, such as the customs of a community today or long ago

questions.q: True or False? 'Newspapers are one of the sources historians use when they study recent history.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says that when historians study recent history (usually the last two or three centuries), newspapers are another source; for the last few decades electronic media can also be consulted.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: newspapers are a source for recent history, the last two or three centuries

questions.q: A museum in Lucknow has three finds from a 3,000-year-old village: (i) skeletons from a burial, (ii) cooking pots with dark material stuck inside them, and (iii) layers of mud from a nearby dried-up lake. For each find, name the kind of scientific study mentioned in the chapter that could be used on it, and what it could help us learn.
questions.a: (i) Skeletons: studies of the genetics of ancient people, to learn how features were passed down from one generation to the next among these people. (ii) Pots: chemical studies of excavated materials, to learn what the pots, or what was left in them, were made of. (iii) Lake mud: studies of ancient climates, to learn what the climate was like when the village existed.
s: Skeletons: genetics of ancient people, about features passed down between generations
Pots: chemical studies of excavated materials, about what the material is made of
Lake mud: studies of ancient climates, about the climate of that time

questions.q:
Visitors to a heritage fair ask five questions. For each one, name the specialist from the chapter who is best placed to answer it.
(a) How were the hills around Shillong formed, and what are their rocks made of?
(b) Which animal left this bone that is preserved in rock from millions of years ago?
(c) How do the people of a fishing village in Kerala celebrate their harvest festival today?
(d) What tools did people use at an old settlement that lies buried under this mound?
(e) What does the writing carved on this ancient stone pillar say?
questions.a: (a) A geologist, who studies the physical features of the Earth such as hills, stones and soil. (b) A palaeontologist, who studies fossil remains of plants, animals and humans from millions of years ago. (c) An anthropologist, who studies human societies and cultures, including those of today. (d) An archaeologist, who digs up remains such as tools, pots and bones. (e) An epigraphist, who studies ancient inscriptions.
s: (a) Geologist
(b) Palaeontologist
(c) Anthropologist
(d) Archaeologist
(e) Epigraphist

questions.q: In the way years are labelled across the world today, what does 'BCE' stand for?
questions.a: Before Common Era

Which of the statements is/are correct?

questions.q: What is an era? Name one kind of event that has often marked the beginning of a new era.
questions.a: An era is a distinct period of time. The birth of an important person, or the start of a ruler's reign, has often marked the beginning of a new era.
s: States that an era is a distinct period of time
Names the birth of an important person or the start of a ruler's reign

questions.q: True or False? 'A pañchānga is a book that only gives the dates of festivals.' Give the verdict and the correct statement.
questions.a: False. A pañchānga is a book of tables that lists the days of each month along with related astronomical data; it often also gives weather predictions for the year and the dates and timings of festivals.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: it lists the days of each month with astronomical data, and also weather predictions and festival dates

questions.q:
(a) Which years did the label 'AD' use to mark?
(b) What are these years now called across the world?
(c) Write the year in which India gained independence using the new label.
questions.a: (a) AD marked the years after the conventional year of Jesus' birth (it is short for a Latin phrase). (b) They are now called the Common Era, or CE. (c) 1947 CE.

(b) Common Era (CE)

questions.q:
A running club in Pune holds its 'Leap Day Run' only on 29 February. Its first run was in 1996. In the Gregorian calendar a leap year comes every four years, but a century year is a leap year only if it is a multiple of 400.
(a) List the years from 1996 to 2012 in which the run was held.
(b) 2000 is a century year. Explain why the run still took place that year.
(c) Will there be a Leap Day Run in 2100? Give the reason.
(d) How many runs were held from 1996 to 2024, both years included?
questions.a: (a) 1996, 2000, 2004, 2008 and 2012. (b) A century year is a leap year if it is a multiple of 400, and 2000 = 5 x 400, so 2000 had 29 February. (c) No. 2100 is a century year that is not a multiple of 400 (2100 / 400 = 5.25), so it has no 29 February. (d) 1996, 2000, 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020, 2024: 8 runs.
s: (b) Explains that 2000 is a multiple of 400, so it is a leap year
(c) Says no, because 2100 is not a multiple of 400
(d) Counts 8 runs from 1996 to 2024

questions.q: A seal was made in 4 BCE and a coin in 6 CE. How many years apart were they made?
questions.a: 9 years

Assertion (A): From 1200 CE to 1500 CE, 299 years pass.
Reason (R): The Gregorian calendar has no year zero; the year 1 CE follows immediately after the year 1 BCE.

questions.q:

(b) Why do we subtract 1 in this calculation?

questions.q: True or False? 'From 6 BCE to 4 CE, 10 years pass.' Give the verdict and the correct working.
questions.a: False. There is no year zero, so the years are 6 + 4 - 1 = 9, not 10.

Correct working: 6 + 4 - 1 = 9 years, as there is no year zero

questions.q:
Arun writes in his notebook: 'From 120 BCE to 80 CE is 120 - 80 = 40 years.'
(a) What has Arun done wrong?
(b) Work out the correct number of years.
questions.a: (a) One date is BCE and the other CE, so the two numbers must be added and then 1 subtracted (there is no year zero); Arun subtracted one number from the other. (b) 120 + 80 - 1 = 199 years.
s: (a) Says that for a BCE and a CE date the numbers are added and 1 subtracted, not one taken from the other

questions.q:
Find the number of years between each pair of dates.
(a) 8 BCE and 12 CE
(b) 300 CE and 900 CE
(c) 70 BCE and 1 CE
s: (a) 19 years
(b) 600 years
(c) 70 years

questions.q:
A copper plate was made in 360 BCE. A stupa was built exactly 500 years after it.
(a) Was the stupa built in a BCE year or a CE year? Explain.
(b) Find the year in which the stupa was built.
(c) Check your answer using the rule for counting years between a BCE date and a CE date.
questions.a: (a) CE: going forward from 360 BCE, the BCE years run out after 360 years, which is less than 500, so the stupa's year is in the CE. (b) 360 + year - 1 = 500, so the year is 500 - 360 + 1 = 141 CE (not 140 CE, as there is no year zero). (c) Check: 360 + 141 - 1 = 500 years.
s: (a) CE, because 360 is less than 500
(b) Finds 141 CE, adding back 1 for the missing year zero

questions.q:
Taking the present year as 2026 CE, find how many years ago each object was made.
(a) A carved door made in 1526 CE
(b) A coin made in 64 BCE
(c) A clay pot made in 1000 BCE
(d) A seal made in 12 BCE
(e) A copper plate made in 826 CE
s: (a) 500 years
(b) 2,089 years
(c) 3,025 years
(d) 2,037 years
(e) 1,200 years

questions.q:
A town in Madhya Pradesh is planning a heritage walk with four stops. Stop 1 is a rock-cut water tank made in 640 BCE. Stop 2 is a hoard of coins buried in 215 BCE. Stop 3 is a copper plate engraved in 378 CE. Stop 4 is a temple built in 1104 CE. The guide is writing a signboard for each stop, taking the present year as 2026 CE.
(a) How many years separate Stop 2 and Stop 3?
(b) How many years old is the water tank at Stop 1?
(c) The guide's board at Stop 2 says the coins are '2,241 years old'. Is this right? If not, correct it.
(d) To save time, the town wants to drop one stop but still have the walk cover more than 1,500 years from its oldest to its newest stop. Which stop or stops could be dropped? Show the working.
questions.a: (a) 215 + 378 - 1 = 592 years. (b) 640 + 2026 - 1 = 2,665 years. (c) No. The guide added 215 + 2026 but forgot to subtract 1 for the missing year zero; the coins are 2,240 years old. (d) Keeping both Stop 1 and Stop 4 gives 640 + 1104 - 1 = 1,743 years. Dropping Stop 1 leaves 215 + 1104 - 1 = 1,318 years and dropping Stop 4 leaves 640 + 378 - 1 = 1,017 years, both under 1,500. So only Stop 2 or Stop 3 can be dropped.
s: (a) 592 years
(b) 2,665 years
(c) Not right: 1 was not subtracted; the correct age is 2,240 years
(d) Compares the spans (1,743; 1,318; 1,017) and decides only Stop 2 or Stop 3 can be dropped

questions.q:
Match each period in Column A with the years it covers in Column B.

What is a century? Which years make up the 21st century CE?
questions.a: A century is any period of 100 years. The 21st century CE runs from 2001 to 2100.

States that the 21st century CE runs from 2001 to 2100

questions.q: True or False? 'The year 650 BCE falls in the 7th century BCE.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Centuries BCE are counted backward from 1 BCE, so the 7th century BCE covers 700 BCE to 601 BCE, and 650 BCE lies within it.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the 7th century BCE covers 700 BCE to 601 BCE, which includes 650 BCE

questions.q:
A seal found at a site is dated 2450 BCE.
(a) In which century BCE was it made?
(b) In which millennium BCE was it made?
(c) A classmate says it belongs to the 24th century BCE because 2450 begins with 24. Explain why this is wrong.
questions.a: (a) The 25th century BCE, which covers 2500 BCE to 2401 BCE. (b) The 3rd millennium BCE, which covers 3000 BCE to 2001 BCE. (c) The 24th century BCE covers only 2400 BCE to 2301 BCE; 2450 BCE lies further back in time than 2400 BCE, so it falls in the 25th century BCE (the century number is one more than the leading digits, as 1757 CE is in the 18th century CE).
s: (a) 25th century BCE (2500 to 2401 BCE)
(b) 3rd millennium BCE (3000 to 2001 BCE)
(c) Explains that the 24th century BCE is 2400 to 2301 BCE, so 2450 BCE is outside it

questions.q: Dev says: 'The 10th century CE and the 10th century BCE are both made up of the years numbered 901 to 1000, so on a timeline both start with 901 and end with 1000.' Is Dev right, wrong or partly right? Explain.
questions.a: Partly right. The numbers are the same: the 10th century CE is 901 CE to 1000 CE, and the 10th century BCE is 1000 BCE to 901 BCE. But the order on a timeline is not the same: BCE years are counted backward from 1 BCE, so the 10th century BCE starts (earliest) with 1000 BCE and ends with 901 BCE, while the 10th century CE starts with 901 CE and ends with 1000 CE.
s: Verdict: partly right
Gives the years of both centuries: 901-1000 CE and 1000-901 BCE
Explains that the BCE century runs from 1000 BCE to 901 BCE because BCE years count backward

questions.q:
A class has five dates to put on a timeline: 1505 CE, 51 BCE, 1550 BCE, 15 CE and 150 BCE.
(a) Arrange them from the earliest to the latest.
(b) Name the century of 51 BCE and the century of 15 CE.
(c) Which two of the five dates fall in the same millennium? Name the millennium.
(d) A student says 1550 BCE and 1505 CE are both in the 15th century because both begin with 15. Correct him.
questions.a: (a) 1550 BCE, 150 BCE, 51 BCE, 15 CE, 1505 CE. (b) 51 BCE is in the 1st century BCE (100 to 1 BCE); 15 CE is in the 1st century CE (1 to 100 CE). (c) 150 BCE and 51 BCE, both in the 1st millennium BCE (1000 to 1 BCE). (d) Both are in fact 16th-century dates, but in different eras: 1550 BCE is in the 16th century BCE (1600 to 1501 BCE) and 1505 CE is in the 16th century CE (1501 to 1600 CE).
s: (a) Orders 1550 BCE, 150 BCE, 51 BCE, 15 CE, 1505 CE
(b) 1st century BCE and 1st century CE
(c) 150 BCE and 51 BCE, in the 1st millennium BCE
(d) 1550 BCE is in the 16th century BCE and 1505 CE in the 16th century CE

questions.q: At an old fort town in Rajasthan, a student writes down three things: (i) carved stone panels on the main gateway, (ii) a copper plate kept in the town temple, and (iii) a ballad about the fort that the elders still sing. Using the chapter's chart, place each one in its main group of sources and, where the chart has one, its sub-group.
questions.a: (i) The carved panels are Artistic Sources (panels). (ii) The copper plate is an Archaeological Source, in the sub-group Inscriptions. (iii) The ballad is an Oral Source (folklore).

(ii) Copper plate: Archaeological Sources, Inscriptions
(iii) Ballad: Oral Sources, folklore

questions.q:
The chapter compares the sources of history to a jigsaw puzzle.
(a) What does each object or structure stand for in this comparison?
(b) What does it mean when the jigsaw pieces match?
(c) What must historians do when the pieces do not match?
questions.a: (a) Each object or structure is like one piece of the jigsaw puzzle. (b) The sources confirm each other. (c) The sources give contradictory information, so historians must decide which source they can trust more.
s: (a) Each source is one piece of the puzzle
(b) The sources confirm each other
(c) Historians decide which source they can trust more

questions.q:
A museum in Bhopal has opened a new 'Sources of History' gallery. On display are 6 coins, 3 copper plates, 2 manuscripts, a model of a mound, a model of a monument, 14 pieces of pottery and toys, 5 figurines and 2 burials. There are also 4 sculptures and 3 panels, and an audio corner that plays 7 folk songs recorded in nearby villages. The gallery has no paintings.
(a) How many items in the gallery belong to the sub-group Inscriptions?
(b) To which main group of sources do the 7 folk songs belong?
(c) How many items belong to Artistic Sources?
(d) Which sub-group of Archaeological Sources has the most items in the gallery?
questions.a: (a) Coins, copper plates and manuscripts: 6 + 3 + 2 = 11. (b) Oral Sources (folklore). (c) Sculptures and panels: 4 + 3 = 7. (d) Excavations: pottery and toys, figurines and burials make 14 + 5 + 2 = 21, more than Inscriptions (11) and Structures (2).
s: (a) 11 items (coins, copper plates, manuscripts)
(b) Oral Sources
(c) 7 items (sculptures and panels)
(d) Excavations, with 21 items

questions.q:
A historian wants to find when the village of Kesarpur was founded. She has three sources. (i) A copper plate in the village temple records a grant of land to settle the new village in 1342 CE. (ii) A family bard recites a genealogy that names 20 generations from the village's founder to the present head of the family. (iii) Pots and burials dug out of a mound at the edge of the village, which scientists date to about 1300 to 1350 CE.
(a) Place each source in its main group and sub-group using the chapter's chart.
(b) Which two sources confirm each other? Explain.
(c) Taking one generation as 30 years and the present year as 2026 CE, in about which year does the genealogy place the founding?
(d) Does the genealogy confirm or contradict the other two sources, and by about how many years?
(e) Which founding date should the historian trust more? Justify your choice.
questions.a: (a) The copper plate is Archaeological, Inscriptions; the genealogy is an Oral Source (genealogical); the pots and burials are Archaeological, Excavations. (b) The copper plate (1342 CE) and the finds from the mound (about 1300 to 1350 CE), since 1342 lies inside the scientists' range. (c) 20 x 30 = 600 years, and 2026 - 600 = 1426 CE. (d) It contradicts them: 1426 - 1342 = 84 years later than the copper plate. (e) The date of about 1342 CE, because two different kinds of source match like jigsaw pieces, while the genealogy rests on an assumed 30 years per generation and so gives only a rough date.
s: (a) Copper plate: Inscriptions; genealogy: Oral; pots and burials: Excavations
(b) Copper plate and mound finds confirm each other
(c) 600 years back gives about 1426 CE
(d) Contradicts, by about 84 years
(e) Trusts about 1342 CE, as two sources agree and the generation count is only an estimate

questions.q:
A library has two old books. One is an ancient Indian text on medicines made from herbs. The other was written by a merchant from a faraway land, describing the markets he saw while travelling through an Indian kingdom.

(b) Place the second book in the same way.
questions.a: (a) Indian Literature, scientific and technological texts. (b) Foreign Accounts, travelogues.

(b) Foreign Accounts, travelogues

questions.q:
(a) Under which branch of Literary Sources does the chart list poems and plays?
(b) Under which branch does it list historical chronicles?
(c) A poem is written in an old language that few people read today. Whose help, named in the chapter, would a historian need to understand it?
questions.a: (a) Indian Literature. (b) Foreign Accounts. (c) Experts in literature and languages.
s: (a) Indian Literature
(b) Foreign Accounts
(c) Experts in literature and languages

questions.q:
A college library in Pune keeps old books for history students. Its list shows 14 travelogues, 6 historical chronicles, 9 collections of stories, 11 books of poems and plays, 5 scientific and technological texts, 3 historical texts and 8 volumes of the Vedas and Itihasas. A student has time to read only 10 of these books for a project called 'How visitors from other lands saw our region'.
(a) How many of the library's books are Foreign Accounts?
(b) How many are Indian Literature?
(c) Which branch has more books, and by how many?
(d) Should the student choose her 10 books from the larger branch because it has more books? Decide and justify, saying whether one Indian book could still be useful to her.
questions.a: (a) Travelogues and historical chronicles: 14 + 6 = 20. (b) 9 + 11 + 5 + 3 + 8 = 36. (c) Indian Literature, by 36 - 20 = 16 books. (d) No. Her topic is how visitors from other lands saw the region, which is what Foreign Accounts (travelogues and chronicles) give, so most of her 10 books should come from those 20, whatever the size of the other branch. Still, one Indian book, such as a historical text, would be useful: comparing it with the visitors' accounts shows whether the sources confirm or contradict each other, like matching jigsaw pieces.
s: (a) 20 Foreign Accounts
(b) 36 Indian Literature books
(c) Indian Literature, by 16
(d) Decides to choose mainly Foreign Accounts because of the topic, and that one Indian text helps check the accounts

(a) Would this fit the way the chapter says such early farming communities worked? Explain.

s: (a) No, because land was sown and harvested collectively with no individual ownership
(b) The chieftains (leaders)

questions.q:
(a) What does the word 'afterlife' mean?
(b) Why did early humans live in bands or groups?
(c) What did early humans sometimes exchange with other groups?
questions.a: (a) A life that begins after death. (b) They faced many challenges from nature, so they lived in bands to help each other. (c) Simple ornaments, such as stone or shell beads and pendants made of animal teeth.
s: (a) A life that begins after death
(b) To help each other face the challenges of nature
(c) Ornaments such as beads and animal-teeth pendants

questions.q: Compare a band of early hunter-gatherers with a settled farming village of later times on these five points, using the chapter: (a) where they lived, (b) how they got their food, (c) how the group was run and how land was used, (d) the tools and technologies they used, (e) what they exchanged with other groups.
questions.a: (a) Bands lived in temporary camps, rock shelters or caves; farming villages settled down, often near rivers for water and fertile soil. (b) Bands hunted and collected edible plants and fruits; villagers cultivated cereals and grains and domesticated animals such as cattle and goats. (c) Bands lived in groups to help each other; in villages, chieftains were responsible for the people's well-being and the lands were sown and harvested collectively. (d) Bands used fire and stone tools such as axes, blades and arrowheads; villages also had pottery and metal (copper first, iron later) for durable tools, objects of daily use and ornaments. (e) Bands sometimes exchanged ornaments such as beads and pendants; villages exchanged goods, mostly food, clothing and tools, through networks between villages.
s: (a) Temporary camps, rock shelters or caves against settled villages near rivers
(b) Hunting and gathering against growing crops and keeping animals
(c) Bands helping each other against chieftains and land worked collectively
(d) Stone tools and fire against pottery and copper, later iron
(e) Occasional exchange of ornaments against exchange of food, clothing and tools

questions.q:
Archaeologists study two sites in a river valley in Karnataka. Site P is a rock shelter 3 km from the river. It has 120 stone blades, 40 arrowheads, 25 shell beads, 3 pendants made of animal teeth, ash from old fires and paintings of deer on its walls, but no pots and no grain. Site Q is on the river bank. It has 300 pieces of pottery, 60 copper objects, burnt grains of a cereal, bones of cattle and goats, and the remains of 35 huts. No iron is found at either site.
(a) Which site was most likely used by a band of hunter-gatherers? Give one piece of evidence.
(b) What do the grain and the cattle and goat bones at Site Q show about its people?
(c) Why might the people of Site Q have chosen to live on the river bank?
(d) A trainee says Site Q probably belongs to a later stage of human history than Site P. Do you agree? Justify with two pieces of evidence from the data.
questions.a: (a) Site P: it has only stone blades and arrowheads, used for hunting, and no pots or grain. (b) They cultivated cereals and had domesticated animals such as cattle and goats. (c) The river gave water, and the soil near rivers is more fertile, which made growing crops easier. (d) Agree. Site Q shows farming (grain, cattle and goats), which began after the last Ice Age, and new technologies, pottery and copper, which came later still; Site P shows only the stone tools, ornaments and rock art of hunter-gatherer bands.
s: (a) Site P, with evidence such as stone tools and no pots or grain
(b) They grew cereals and domesticated animals
(c) Water and more fertile soil near the river
(d) Agrees, citing farming and pottery or copper at Q against stone tools only at P
